title: Are You Still the Agent I Authorized? Earned Authority under a Fixed Ceiling for Evolving Agents
summary:
Long-lived AI agents increasingly evolve after deployment by retaining experience, acquiring skills and tools, revising workflows, delegating work, and moving across task phases. This improves adaptation but creates a distinct authorization problem. Tool-enabled agents can turn model errors and prompt injections into consequential external actions; when evolution occurs under a live grant, the subject exercising that authority or the context in which it acts may no longer match what the user evaluated. Evolution can change both the effects reachable under an old grant and the authority required by the task, which may rise, fall, or become incomparable. Existing tool policies constrain actions but do not determine when a grant survives this change.
  We formulate authorization continuity: when does an existing grant remain valid, how may active authority change, and what boundary must never move? Our state-bound model fixes a transition envelope and an immutable effect ceiling at grant time. The envelope determines whether the grant survives a mutation; below the ceiling, authority may contract freely and expand only under specified evidence conditions. We distinguish requested from realized effects and prove that, under complete mediation, sound effect abstraction, attenuating delegation, and monitor integrity, mutation cannot amplify protected effects beyond the user-issued ceiling. Agent-produced evidence may allocate authority below the ceiling but cannot raise it. Finally, we map six mutation classes to their authorization consequences.

title: Enabling Fully Integer-Only Inference for Lightweight Detection Transformers
summary: Vision Transformer detectors now approach the accuracy of CNNs but remain difficult to deploy on NPUs and microcontrollers because key components, including deformable attention, feature fusion, and nonlinear activation functions, are not natively compatible with integer arithmetic. Existing quantized detectors either retain operators such as Softmax, GELU, and LayerNorm or focus on heavyweight backbones, leaving lightweight detection transformers without an end-to-end integer implementation. We address this gap with I-LW-DETR, the first fully integer-only lightweight DETR, in which every operation in the forward pass, including transformer nonlinearities, is executed in integer arithmetic. I-LW-DETR is built upon three key components: a scale-preserving split convolution that assigns independent activation scale to each branch of the multi-scale projector; SD-ShiftGELU, a sign-dependent GELU approximation that preserves element-wise behavior while avoiding the accuracy degradation; and a constrained Shiftmax that maintains stable Softmax normalization. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed quantization pipeline consistently produces efficient fully integer-only models across different model scales. Across all model scales, the proposed pipeline incurs only a moderate accuracy degradation while reducing the model size by approximately $3.6\times$ and the computational cost by more than one order of magnitude.

title: Convergence of entropy-conservative summation-by-parts discretizations to smooth solutions of hyperbolic conservation laws
comments: All code required to reproduce the numerical results is available online at https://github.com/ranocha/2026_convergence_sbp and https://zenodo.org/doi/10.5281/zenodo.21672279
summary: Although entropy-based summation-by-parts (SBP) discretizations of hyperbolic conservation laws are widely used for their robustness and stability properties, there are very few results on their convergence. We extend a recent convergence analysis of Worku, Del Rey Fernández, and Zingg (2026, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2603.18369) in two ways. First, instead of allowing only hyperbolic conservation laws whose fluxes are homogeneous and have globally bounded second derivatives (a restriction essentially to linear or quadratic fluxes), we consider general hyperbolic systems with strictly convex entropy and source terms depending on time and space. Second, instead of requiring a special class of SBP operators, we consider a general framework of diagonal-norm SBP operators on curved meshes, including finite differences, continuous and discontinuous Galerkin methods. Since the error analysis is based on a discrete relative entropy, it is restricted to smooth solutions. To enable a unified treatment of conservation laws, we restrict the analysis to periodic boundary conditions. Numerical results demonstrate that the predicted convergence rates are sharp in general, but can be improved for special cases such as discontinuous Galerkin methods with even polynomial degree and multi-block finite difference methods. An optimal analysis is expected to require more sophisticated arguments specialized to the class of methods instead of the general framework of SBP operators used in this work.
comment: All code required to reproduce the numerical results is available online at https://github.com/ranocha/2026_convergence_sbp and https://zenodo.org/doi/10.5281/zenodo.21672279

title: Failure Detection for Surgical Robot Imitation Policies via Flow-Matching World Modeling
comments: 8 pages, 4 figures. Revised following peer review. Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Imitation learning has shown increasing promise for autonomous robotic surgery, yet safe deployment remains challenging due to the safety-critical nature of surgical tasks and the complexity and variability of surgical environments. Failure detection is therefore an essential safeguard, but its development remains difficult due to the challenges of scarce failure data, highly variable manipulation dynamics, and the need to balance missed detections against disruptive false alarms. To address these challenges, we introduce FoMo-FD (Flow-Matching World Model for Failure Detection), a failure detection method that learns nominal short-horizon visual dynamics with an action-conditioned flow-matching world model. FoMo-FD scores the inverse-transport nonconformity of observed endpoint latents, enabling window-level detection of deviations from learned nominal dynamics without requiring failure demonstrations. Detection thresholds are obtained by conformal calibration on successful policy rollouts, yielding task-specific alarms without assuming future failure types. We evaluate FoMo-FD on four surgically relevant manipulation tasks with twenty failure modes across simulation and real-robot experiments using the da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK). In the wrist view, the main model achieves a 95.6% failure detection rate (FDR) at a 2.5% false alarm rate (FAR), exceeding the FDR of the evaluated observation-based, action-based, and vision-language baselines and alternative scores from the same world model. Across four training seeds, mean wrist-view FDR and FAR are 93.4% and 4.7%, respectively. Online replay yields a mean onset-relative detection delay of 0.98 s for wrist-view failures detected offline. Project website: https://janusmaple.github.io/FoMoFD/
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Revised following peer review. Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)

title: Mechanical Modeling of Braided Neurovascular Flow Diverters using a Beam-to-Beam and Beam-to-Surface Contact Formulation
summary: Braided neurovascular flow diverters are widely used for the endovascular treatment of intracranial aneurysms. Their mechanical response and deployed configuration are governed by the interaction of many slender, interwoven wires, which makes the numerical simulation of the complete device a challenging problem. This work presents a detailed mechanical model of complete braided flow diverters that integrates geometrically exact beam mechanics and contact mechanics into one consistent implicit finite element formulation. Every wire is modeled as a geometrically exact Simo-Reissner beam, which consistently describes large rotations and curved reference configurations. The interactions between the wires are captured by a beam-to-beam contact formulation with a history-dependent gap function that prevents unintended wire crossings. The interaction with surrounding tubular structures, such as microcatheters or crimping devices, is captured by a beam-to-surface contact formulation. A parametric description of interwoven braided geometries enables systematic control of design parameters such as wire count, braiding angle, device length, and interweaving pattern. The model is assessed by means of three test cases from the literature. A tensile test investigates the length-diameter relation and the axial force response, and a radial compression test addresses the pressure-diameter behavior. A stepwise compression example evaluates geometry-sensitive quantities, including local wire distance, helix angle, porosity, and metal coverage ratio. The results show that the model captures both the characteristic mechanical response and clinically relevant geometric quantities of braided flow diverters.

title: AiFlow: Construction-to-Retirement Conformance for Versioned LLM Services
summary: A live update can preserve the topology and output of a large language model (LLM) workflow while bypassing a filter's queue and concurrency limits. A background task can use the old version after its caller returns. AiFlow links construction, invocation and retirement through an executable contract. Each admitted request captures an action bound to the checked operators. The service certifies the call's terminal outcome and the release of its registered work. Once new calls can no longer capture the version, the owner checks these certificates and remaining local resources before retirement. Strict publication pauses admission while old calls drain. Deferred publication can admit calls to the successor before its predecessor retires. We evaluated two stateless linear workflows in one Java virtual machine. Under strict publication, we repeated three injected fault scenarios three times per check configuration. An observation counted as contained if neither unguarded execution nor premature replacement occurred. With construction or completion checking alone, six of nine fault observations met this criterion. With both checks, all nine did. A separately implemented coordinator matched AiFlow on the lifecycle outcome, service call count and reclamation decision in all 24 tested pairs. With updates every 400 ms, deferred publication met the 500 ms deadline more often at both loads. We measured the share of all offered requests that met the deadline on the latest scheduled version due at return. Strict publication led at 80 requests/s and deferred publication at 20 requests/s. Both policies use the same local evidence for retirement.

title: A Graph Signal Processing Perspective on Numerical Sequence Representations in LLM In-Context Learning
summary: Pretrained large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated in-context learning (ICL) capabilities for numerical inference over sequences serialized as text. Prior work has identified and characterized this form of numerical inference primarily through output-level evaluations such as prediction error. However, how numerical information is organized within LLM representations remains much less understood. To study this internal organization, we adopt a graph signal processing perspective in which attention induces a weighted graph over tokens, while token hidden states define signals on its nodes. Quantitative graph-spectral diagnostics and qualitative token-graph visualizations reveal that representations become more clearly differentiated by input dynamical complexity as context length increases. Simpler inputs produce attention-induced token graphs with stronger global connectivity and smoother, spectrally concentrated hidden-state signals, whereas more complex inputs produce more localized graphs and hidden-state signals with broader spectral support and greater high-frequency energy. These diagnostics and visualizations offer an interpretable view of the internal structure associated with numerical ICL, beyond what output-level prediction error alone reveals. Together, these findings point to systematic, context-dependent internal signatures associated with numerical ICL that are qualitatively conserved across model families.

title: ED-DiT: Physics-Guided Diffusion Pretraining for Transferable Molecular Representations from Electron Density
comments: 16 pages, 9 figures, 7 tables, including supplementary material
summary: Pretraining has shown strong potential for learning transferable representations, yet it remains underexplored for electron-density-based molecular learning. Electron density provides a continuous three-dimensional description of molecular electronic structure, capturing both local spatial patterns and global physical quantities. This raises a key question: can electron-density fields be used for self-supervised pretraining to learn a shared representation that transfers across diverse electronic-structure-related tasks? We propose ED-DiT, a physics-guided Diffusion Transformer for self-supervised pretraining on electron-density point clouds. ED-DiT learns reusable representations by reconstructing corrupted and partially masked log-density fields across diffusion noise levels. An electron-number consistency constraint is further introduced to preserve the total electronic mass. The pretrained encoder can be adapted to property prediction, open-/closed-shell classification, molecule-electron-density retrieval, and molecule-conditioned electron-density prediction. Experiments on six EDBench tasks show that ED-DiT consistently outperforms the same architecture trained from scratch, especially under limited supervision. For molecule-conditioned electron-density prediction, it reduces RMSE from 2.2474 to 1.3753 and surpasses the available baseline. With only 10% labels, it improves orbital energy prediction RMSE from 0.0293 to 0.0138. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of physics-guided electron-density pretraining for learning transferable molecular representations.
comment: 16 pages, 9 figures, 7 tables, including supplementary material

title: NOLLI: A Difficulty-Calibrated English-Korean Puzzle Benchmark
summary: We introduce NOLLI, a procedurally generated, difficulty-calibrated English-Korean puzzle benchmark with 15 puzzle types (25 tasks; 7,500 items). Each instance is seed-regenerable, has a verified unique solution, and is scored deterministically. We calibrate difficulty behaviorally by tuning generator parameters to target accuracy bands on a reference model. NOLLI has three task families: matched direct translations, script adaptations over Hangul jamo (sub-syllabic letters), and Korean-only cultural or orthographic tasks. We evaluate 15 frontier, open-weight, and Korean-developed models; gap analyses use the 12 above a 3% overall-accuracy floor. On matched direct translations, English and Korean accuracy is equivalent within a prespecified $\pm 10$ percentage-point margin. Script adaptations behave differently: Korean Cipher trails English by up to 68.7 percentage points, while Cryptarithmetic over the same jamo shows no systematic Korean penalty, and Jamo Composition strongly correlates with Korean Cipher performance. Korean-only tasks are also heterogeneous: rule-application performance varies across models, while Kinship remains below each non-floor model's Korean direct-task baseline. Finally, structural size does not increase from Easy to Hard in 7 of 15 types, showing that size alone is an unreliable proxy for empirical difficulty.

title: Fisher-R1: Training LLM Agents for Reliable Hypothesis Testing
summary: Reliable hypothesis testing is the foundation of many empirical scientific claims. Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to automate this process, as they can inspect datasets, generate code, and produce analyses end-to-end. However, we show that they frequently make subtle inferential errors that lead to incorrect conclusions despite correctly executed analyses. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this failure mode, as they rarely assess whether a reported p-value is statistically valid given the assumptions underlying the data. We address this gap by building P-Bench, a benchmark comprising 425 open-ended, realistic hypothesis-testing tasks spanning economics, biology, and medicine. Each task requires an agent to select a statistical method, compute a p-value, and draw a conclusion given only a scientific hypothesis and a dataset. We further introduce Fisher-R1, an open-weight LLM agent trained for rigorous hypothesis testing using synthetic tasks and reinforcement learning. On P-Bench, Fisher-R1-14B substantially improves over its backbone and outperforms strong proprietary and open-source baselines, including GPT-5.4 and DeepSeekV4-Pro, achieving a 21% average relative improvement in single-trial success over DeepSeek-V4-Pro, with gains up to 26% on the most challenging tasks. Our results demonstrate that current LLM agents lack reliable statistical reasoning for hypothesis testing and that reinforcement learning on tasks with verified statistical reward substantially improves reliability.

title: Event-Time Hybrid Optimal Control for Robotic Table Tennis Serves
summary: Robotic table tennis serves require high ball velocity and spin while respecting the robot's kinodynamic limits. Unlike rally strokes, a valid serve must also bounce on the server's side and clear the net, yielding a hybrid system with nonlinear flight and impact dynamics. We formulate spin-controlled serve generation as an event-time \ac{OCP} that optimizes the racket impact velocity and orientation together with the bounce, net-crossing, and landing times, enabling direct enforcement at phase boundaries of table-bounce and net-clearance constraints. The racket velocity and orientation are then converted into a complete kinodynamically feasible motion through a second \ac{OCP} enforcing joint-position, velocity, and torque limits. We evaluate the method numerically and on a KUKA Agilus robot. Compared with a fixed-step formulation with root localization, the proposed event-time formulation reduces the median solve time by a factor of 4.1 while maintaining comparable landing accuracy, spin accuracy, and serve validity. Real-robot experiments demonstrate controlled placement and topspin, backspin, and sidespin serves, with a mean landing error of $13.1 \pm 7.3$~cm and spin rates up to 30~rps. These results show that event-time optimal control efficiently generates physically valid, kinodynamically feasible serves while accounting for nonlinear aerodynamic and impact effects.

title: Fine-Grained AC$^0$ Lower Bounds for $k$-OV, $k$-XOR, and $k$-SUM via Colored Subgraph Isomorphism
comments: Improved and simplified depth-3 result. Omitted non-critical results to substantially simplify paper narrative
summary:
We study the circuit cost of selecting $k$ objects satisfying orthogonality, zero XOR, or modular zero SUM. Our main lower bounds in nonuniform AC$^0$ use a common framework of depth-zero projections from colored subgraph isomorphism. The projections use dimension, row count, or bit width $O(k\log n)$ and preserve circuit size, depth, and gate orientation. Stronger lower bounds for suitable source patterns transfer through the same framework to all three targets. Our XOR lower bounds require odd $k$.
  For every fixed depth $d$ and sufficiently large fixed $k$, we prove unconditional lower bounds $n^{Ω(k)}$ for OV and $(n/k)^{Ω(k)}$ for XOR and SUM, with an absolute constant in the exponent independent of $d$ and $k$; only the threshold on $n$ may depend on $(d,k)$. For $k\to\infty$ with $k=n^{o(1)}$, combining our projections with Beame's small-clique lower bound yields $n^{Ω_d(\min\{\sqrt{k},\log n\})}$ at every fixed depth $d$. For circuits of depth at most three with either type of output gate, we strengthen the exponent to $Ω(k)$.
  At dimension, row count, or bit width $Θ(k\log n)$ with sufficiently large constant factors, all three problems admit depth-three circuits with a top OR gate. Their sizes match our lower bounds for unrestricted depth three up to constants in the exponent for sufficiently large $k$ and $n\ge k^C$ with a suitable constant $C>1$.
comment: Improved and simplified depth-3 result. Omitted non-critical results to substantially simplify paper narrative

title: Adaptive Volumetric Parameterization of Simply Connected 3-Manifolds with Applications
summary: Volumetric parameterization, the process of mapping a 3-manifold onto a simplified volumetric domain, is important for many tasks in computer graphics and imaging science. However, most prior volumetric parameterization approaches have only utilized standardized domains such as a solid ball regardless of the overall shape of the given 3-manifolds, which introduces significant geometric distortion and affects the subsequent shape processing and analysis tasks. To overcome this issue, in this work we propose a novel volumetric parameterization framework for simply connected 3-manifolds. Specifically, the proposed framework jointly controls local shape and mass distortions, while adapting the target domain during the optimization process. It enables three progressively more flexible target-domain settings for the parameterization: a prescribed solid ellipsoid, a volume-normalized adaptive ellipsoid with variable radii, and a sea-embedded free-boundary domain. For each setting, the parameterization algorithm consists of a 3D quasi-conformality shape update, a diffusion-based density-equalizing update, and a geometric correction procedure for removing element foldings, thereby allowing for volumetric parameterizations with different desired effects. Experimental results are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework. Moreover, our framework can be easily applied to multiresolution and localized adaptive volumetric remeshing, volumetric registration, and volumetric morphing. Altogether, our work provides a new way for the representation, processing, and analysis of 3-manifolds.

title: AVA-Encoder: Learning to Represent Videos via Reconstruction-Driven Agentic Self-Evolution
summary: Agentic video creation systems remain far from cinematic-grade quality: their underlying models struggle to plan how story, characters, visuals, and sound fit together, and high-quality creation trajectories to learn such planning abilities are scarce. Finished human films embody this knowledge, but in a tightly coupled audiovisual form that agents cannot directly read or manipulate. We propose the Agentic Video "Auto-Encoder" (AVA-Encoder), which works backward from human films, turning them into agent-native video representations with reconstruction itself as the sole supervision. It encodes a film into a Film Knowledge Graph (Film KG) of structured-text nodes, typed dependency edges, and linked multimodal assets, then regenerates the film from this graph with a fixed decoder. Crucially, by distilling reconstruction residuals into textual gradients, AVA-Encoder drives a dual-loop self-evolution: an outer loop autonomously discovers a generalizable encoding strategy entirely from unlabeled videos, while an inner loop refines each video's Film KG at test time. AVA-Encoder improves reconstruction fidelity by 20.9 percentage points over the strongest baseline, and its autonomously learned strategy outperforms a human-tuned strategy using 70% fewer prompt tokens. Our representations drive three downstream breakthroughs: (1) Film KGs enable coordinated graph-based editing and (2) improve one-shot video generation across four open-source frameworks, while (3) fine-tuning agents on our reverse-engineered trajectories boosts video creation quality by 38.7%. We release the framework and a dataset of 500 Film KGs with over 27,000 creation trajectories.

title: RA-DPO: Reliability-Aware Preference Optimization and Selective Prediction for Sexism Detection
comments: Accepted to Findings of EACL 2027. Camera-ready version. 20 pages, 6 figures
summary: Sexism detection is subjective, yet most systems reduce multi-annotator labels to a single majority label, discarding annotator agreement and model uncertainty. We propose RA-DPO (Reliability-Aware Direct Preference Optimization), a framework built on standard DPO that combines annotator agreement, model confidence and token-level uncertainty into one reliability score: agreement and token-level uncertainty select training pairs, agreement up-weights them, and the full score decides when the model should abstain. We evaluate on EXIST 2023 and EDOS, fine-tuning gpt-4o and two open-weight 3B models. The score matters most at inference: on gpt-4o, selective prediction lifts RA-DPO to 96.2% accuracy at 50% coverage with true agreement and 88.7% with agreement predicted from text, against 87.9% for its confidence alone, and abstention improves every variant on both corpora. On the open-weight models, however, confidence alone ranks RA-DPO and Standard DPO better than the full score. On the training side, fewer pairs suffice (30% matches full-data DPO on gpt-4o), but size-matched random subsets (50% on gpt-4o, 30% on the 3B models) do as well as reliability-ranked ones.
comment: Accepted to Findings of EACL 2027. Camera-ready version. 20 pages, 6 figures

title: How Powerful are LLMs in Generating Formal Program Specifications?
summary: Formal verification provides strong guarantees of software correctness, but its adoption is limited by the high cost of writing precise formal specifications. While recent large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities in theorem proving and verified code generation, their true ability to generate program specifications remains unclear. Existing evaluations require either verifying implementation conformance or proving semantic equivalence between specifications, both of which are formidably difficult and may conflate proof difficulty with specification quality. To address this problem, we introduce Coins, a Rocq based evaluation framework that assesses specification quality by instantiating specifications under evaluation on trusted test cases and generating concrete proof obligations. This design aligns with the asymmetric nature of formal reasoning, where successful proofs provide reliable evidence while proof failures are inherently ambiguous. Using Coins, we conduct a large scale study on HumanEval with a curated set of human written Rocq specifications. Our results show that specification generation remains a formidable challenge, and that verification complexity can obscure genuine differences in specification quality. Overall, we find that accurate specification evaluation, rather than model scaling alone, is central to understanding the power of LLMs for specification synthesis, and that test case based formal reasoning offers a more faithful and discriminative measure of progress.

title: CrevasseSeg: A Label-Efficient UAV Crevasse Segmentation Framework
summary: Crevasse mapping from uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery supports glaciological research and field safety, but pixel-level annotation requires costly expert effort. We introduce CrevasseSeg, a binary segmentation evaluation framework from the terminus of Borebreen, Svalbard, comprising 2,244 unlabelled UAV orthomosaic tiles for self-supervised/unsupervised fine-tuning and 200 labelled tiles (24 validation, 176 test). We benchmark five self-supervised objectives (BYOL, Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD), Barlow Twins, VICReg and a combined BYOL-JSD) across O-Net, O-Net++ and a DINOv3-initialised O-Net. Frozen features are read out with a linear probe and an XGBoost classifier, both fit only on the 24 validation tiles. At the final decoder block, the two readouts invert. DINOv3 models are mostly the weakest under linear probing, often collapsing to a constant prediction, yet they are the strongest under XGBoost. This pattern does not hold at earlier decoder blocks. UMAP suggests why: DINOv3 fragments pixels into many small, locally interleaved clusters, whereas the convolutional models embed them on a single class-sorted manifold. Satellite-pretrained DINOv3 beats natural-image initialisation for every objective under XGBoost (+9.7 mDSC on average), but not consistently under linear probing. Our pipeline, DINOv3-ViT-L-Sat-O-Net-BYOL-JSD, reaches 74.75 mDSC / 61.16 mIoU (77.04 / 64.28 with a decoder-block ensemble), on par with BYOL alone, and outperforms RGB-pixel ML baselines. However, a frozen DINOv3-Sat encoder with an XGBoost readout alone reaches 77.18 / 64.17. It matches or exceeds every SSL variant and comes within 0.71 mDSC of a fully supervised DINOv3 U-Net, highlighting satellite foundation models as a strong baseline. We release CrevasseSeg as a benchmark for label-efficient segmentation in remote sensing.

title: Making Highway Performance Measures Actionable: A Controllability-Aware Measure of Traffic Congestion
comments: Submitted to Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
summary: Emerging intelligent transportation systems (ITS) show substantial benefit in reducing congestion, emissions, and accidents and enable lower-cost alternatives to highway lane expansion. However, there currently exists no actionable metric by which agencies can assess the improvement potential from these interventions and then invest in infrastructure where it will be most promising. To guide ITS deployment, we introduce controllability-aware performance measures that quantify the upper bound of improvement that speed-based vehicle control can achieve under fixed demand. We operationalize this with controllable congestion, the maximum achievable reduction in system delay from controlling speed limits, which we estimate via a locally optimal receding-horizon optimization framework. This nonlinear optimization framework is grounded in a smooth reformulation of the METANET macroscopic traffic model and solved using model predictive control (MPC). Using both a synthetic scenario and highway data from the I-24 SMART Corridor in Tennessee, we find that controllable congestion is largely independent of total delay, revealing that for two days with nearly identical travel times, controllable congestion varies from 35% to 86%. We further show how the realizable share of this upper bound depends on the operational constraints imposed. On I-24, the minimum posted speed limit has little effect on controllable congestion, while the frequency of speed limit updates and the maximum difference between adjacent gantries have large impacts. This framework allows highway operators to distinguish between congestion that is structurally constrained by capacity and congestion that is highly responsive to ITS, enabling more cost-effective deployment of control-based traffic infrastructure.
comment: Submitted to Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies

title: RoboEdit: Turning Human Videos into Scalable Robot Training Data
comments: 22 pages, 14 figures, 7 tables, including supplementary material. Revised version with additional experiments and implementation details
summary: Collecting robot hand-object interaction data is costly and embodiment-specific, yet abundant human-object videos remain unusable for robot training. We present RoboEdit, a human-to-robot video editing suite that transforms human manipulation videos into action-consistent, physically plausible robot videos with aligned 3D hand states. To enable scalable supervision, we introduce RoboEdit-ADC, an automatic pipeline that reconstructs and retargets 3D interactions from RGB videos across embodiments. This pipeline generates RoboEdit-14M, a large-scale dataset of 174K aligned video pairs (14M frames) spanning seven robot embodiments, diverse scenes, and interaction types. The core editing engine, RoboEdit-Trans, employs cross-embodiment adaptation modules to preserve temporal coherence while adapting appearance and motion. It further integrates a 3D Robot-State Decoder to recover per-frame hand states for structured motion supervision. Experiments show that RoboEdit achieves state-of-the-art editing quality and supports downstream robot control policies in real-world manipulation tasks. Ultimately, the RoboEdit suite unlocks the vast potential of unlabeled human videos, providing scalable, high-fidelity visual and 3D motion supervision for generalizable robot learning.
comment: 22 pages, 14 figures, 7 tables, including supplementary material. Revised version with additional experiments and implementation details

title: OpenTherm: A Unified and Progressive Benchmark for 2.5D/3D-IC Thermal Prediction
comments: 19 pages. v2: benchmark renamed from IC-ThermBench to OpenTherm
summary: Accurate and efficient chip thermal prediction is essential for advanced packaging design. In recent years, deep learning-based thermal predictors have made significant progress, achieving high prediction accuracy while substantially reducing computational costs. However, differences in datasets, simulators, and evaluation protocols hinder direct comparison of existing methods and systematic assessment of their generalization across design variations and cross-package transfer scenarios. We introduce OpenTherm, an open benchmark combining 32,000 established 3D-IC samples with 50,000 new 2.5D chiplet samples generated with the open-source HotSpot simulator. It provides fixed data splits, a common input representation, and shared evaluation tools. Five deployment-aligned Generalization Scopes cover fixed-design workload prediction, within-family layout, material, and cooling exploration, and cross-package out-of-distribution (OOD) transfer with few-shot adaptation. Under a shared protocol, eight model configurations show gradual error growth within known package families. The best MAE increases by 13.7x from the broadest within-family scope to zero-shot cross-package transfer. Larger models do not consistently generalize better, and ten labeled fields per unseen package reduce MAE by 76-93%. Project site: https://github.com/Day333/OpenTherm.
comment: 19 pages. v2: benchmark renamed from IC-ThermBench to OpenTherm

title: On-Policy Self-Distillation in Diffusion Models
comments: Technical Report; Project Page at https://diffusionopsd.github.io GitHub Repo at https://github.com/worldbench/DiffusionOPSD
summary: Reinforcement learning aligns diffusion and flow models with human preferences and task objectives, yet endpoint rewards do not specify how an intermediate denoising prediction should change. We introduce DiffusionOPSD, an on-policy self-distillation framework that converts image-level reward guidance into explicit self-teachers for clean-output predictions at sampled on-policy queries. At each outer iteration, a frozen exponential moving average self-teacher rolls out trajectories to supply low-noise query states and clean-output anchors. Normalized local reward gradients then synthesize bounded positive and negative self-teachers around each anchor. The student policy distills these detached self-teachers under a finite update budget before an online update refreshes the self-teacher, admitting an exact single-branch variant DiffusionOPSD*. Separating self-teacher synthesis from student backpropagation removes the decoder and reward model from student backward passes and makes synthesis and realized gains separately measurable. On SD3.5-M and step-distilled Z-Image-Turbo, DiffusionOPSD and DiffusionOPSD* achieve the best held-out score across all 20 target-reward settings, winning 19 of 20 individually with gains up to 44.0% over the strongest baseline. They also deliver up to 2.57% the base-anchored gain of ReFL and up to 90% single-reward human win rates, while joint multi-reward training transfers zero-shot with up to 81% human win rates. Separately, comprehensive profiling experiments show that DiffusionOPSD and DiffusionOPSD* use up to 63% and 74% fewer GPU-hours per 100 updates than DiffusionNFT and reach baseline terminal quality up to 13.1% faster. Overall, DiffusionOPSD provides a teacher-free paradigm converting rewards into stable intermediate supervision for diffusion post-training.
comment: Technical Report; Project Page at https://diffusionopsd.github.io GitHub Repo at https://github.com/worldbench/DiffusionOPSD

title: LAION-BVD: A 13-Million-Hour Open Video Dataset for Multimodal Pre-training
summary: We present LAION-BVD (LAION - Big Video Dataset), a large-scale open video dataset for multimodal learning, which contains 1.3B platform-specific video URLs collected from CommonCrawl. From these, we download 80M videos with a total duration of 13.5 million hours. The dataset is designed for multimodal pre-training across the video, audio, and image modalities. Using content-aware scene detection, we extract clips for which we synthetically generate video and audio captions. Models trained on these data achieve competitive performance on standard video-text and audio-text benchmarks, with consistent improvements as training or model scale increases. Additionally, we explore video frames as an alternative source of image-text data by extracting scene-changing frames. These frames exhibit a visual distribution distinct from standard web image corpora, and models trained on this dataset achieve strong image-text retrieval performance. We release LAION-BVD to the research community. It significantly expands open access to multimodal videos at an unprecedented scale.

title: SILK: Streaming Authentication with In-Place Checks for Low-bit LLM Inference
summary: A root-of-trust (RoT) supports model authentication at load time but does not guarantee integrity during inference. We present SILK, a quantization-aware in-place integrity framework protecting low-bit large language model (LLM) weights, activations, and KV caches against runtime tampering by embedding keyed checks directly into quantized data. Weight checks are embedded during second-order post-training quantization (GPTQ) to minimize distortion, while runtime tensors use redundant codes or fallback least significant bits (LSBs). An Ascon-based authentication chain absorbs each unit's cover bits into the next unit's authentication state, enabling single-pass verification. A streaming guard permits computation after bounded-strength confirmation and holds results until full authentication. Across evaluated symmetric INT4 models, mean perplexity increases remain below 0.4% with 0.2% weight metadata. Against Dual MAC guards, SILK cuts time overhead on Qwen2.5-0.5B weight reads at 4 B/cycle from 1.95% to 0.41% (Dual MAC-256) and energy-delay product (EDP) overhead at 4-8 B/cycle by 28-69% with DDR (up to 37% with HBM2), with 28% more guard-logic area.

title: Neuromorphic architectures as numerical solvers for computational neuroscience
summary: Neuromorphic computing is closely associated with spiking neuronal networks. However, an alternative class of so-called "rate-based" models arising from computational neuroscience and machine learning forgoes spiking interactions and instead relies on continuous coupling between neurons. Existing neuromorphic implementations designed around spike-based interactions are not well-suited for emulating such models. Here we view the distributed simulation of these models as message-passing algorithms on parallel hardware. Leveraging prior art in numerical algorithms and distributed simulation, we outline steps that enable the design of efficient digital neuromorphic accelerators for non-spiking neuronal models. In particular, we show that multi-bit packets, rather than spikes, are the most efficient communication strategy in packet-switched networks and that compared to basic numerical integration methods, higher-order differential equation solvers decrease both computation and communication costs while achieving lower numerical error, but that these benefits are ultimately limited by arithmetic precision. Using our proposed design principles, we convert an existing neuromorphic architecture into a distributed numerical solver - a spikeless neuromorphic system - for continuously-coupled neuronal models. We thereby demonstrate that our theoretical considerations indeed translate into practical advantages, namely reduced energy consumption and delay.

title: LightFuse: Relightable Interactive Gaussian Scene Reconstruction via Multi-Scan Fusion and 2D Gaussian Ray Tracing
summary: Relightable interactive scene reconstruction aims to build an editable 3D model from scans of different object arrangements, so that novel layouts can be rendered under novel illumination. However, Gaussian-splatting-based methods bake illumination into appearance and thus cannot jointly reconstruct scans captured under different lighting, while existing multi-illumination inverse rendering methods struggle to handle scenes whose geometry changes across captures. We present LightFuse, a 2D Gaussian inverse rendering framework that bridges this gap by extending interactive scene reconstruction with explicit material-illumination decomposition and physically based relighting. LightFuse fuses observations across states to reconstruct a shared background and movable objects. Since geometry optimized by splatting alone is ill-suited for ray-tracing-based inverse rendering, it then performs ray-tracing-oriented geometry refinement to obtain more complete and consistent surfaces. Because rearrangement leaves materials unchanged, we jointly optimize a shared set of materials across all scans under varying illumination, with differentiable one-bounce ray tracing disentangling them from the per-scan environment lighting. Experiments on novel-state relighting of synthetic scenes and novel-state synthesis of captured real scenes show that LightFuse outperforms interactive reconstruction and adapted inverse rendering baselines, improving novel-state relighting PSNR by 6.01 dB over the strongest baseline and achieving the highest PSNR on captured scenes. Project page: https://zhn202.github.io/LightFuse/ .

title: Online Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization Beyond $1/e$ with Feasible Gradient Queries
comments: Completely rewritten: new approach and results
summary: We study adversarial online maximization of nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed sets $K\subseteq[0,1]^d$ when gradients may be queried only at feasible points. The online approximation coefficients $4/9$ (Aggarwal and Lu) and $2\sqrt{3}-3\approx 0.4641$ (Aggarwal and Du) rely on queries along chains that start from the all-ones vector and leave $K$. With every query in $K$, the best known coefficient was $1/e$. We give an online algorithm with coefficient $0.4013$ that, in each round, plays a random action, queries one gradient at a point of $K$, and makes one projection. Its expected approximate regret is $O(RB(1+R)\sqrt{T})$, where $R\le\sqrt{d}$ bounds the norm of points of $K$ and $B$ bounds the gradient norm on $K$. For a budget $\sum_i x_i\le k$, the bound is $O(kB\sqrt{T})$. The algorithm keeps a state $x\in K$, and the analysis applies the coordinate-chain comparison of Aggarwal and Lu inside the box $[0,x]$, which keeps every query feasible. A second comparison, along a path from $0$ in the direction $x$, cancels the extra terms that the box creates. Because the queries are feasible, they can be played, which gives regret $O(T^{2/3})$ under semi-bandit feedback and $O(T^{4/5})$ under bandit feedback with bounded values. Unbiased stochastic gradients with bounded second moment keep the $\sqrt{T}$ rate, and on a fixed function the algorithm attains $0.4013\,\mathrm{OPT}-\varepsilon$ in expectation with $O(1+R^2(1+R)^2B^2/\varepsilon^2)$ feasible gradient queries.
comment: Completely rewritten: new approach and results

title: BuildOcc: A Large Language Model Occupant Agent Platform for Building Energy Research
comments: Accepted manuscript. Published in SoftwareX. 19 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables, 3 appendices. Software: https://github.com/humanbuildingsynergy/BuildOcc. Re-set in the HUBS Lab paper layout (HUBS Lab Paper No. 2026-004); content unchanged
summary: Occupants are a primary source of uncertainty in building energy consumption and management, yet existing occupant behavior models cannot capture adaptive and reasoning responses considering the occupant's personal history, current context, and the type of energy signal being delivered. This study presents BuildOcc, an open-source Python platform that grounds large language model agents in the American Time Use Survey (ATUS), a nationally representative diary dataset covering 16,684 respondents. Through BuildOcc, each simulated occupant agent can be instantiated with a demographic persona drawn from ATUS population statistics, a memory stream that accumulates and reflects on timestep-level observations, and an activity scheduler that samples empirically from ATUS time-at-activity distributions. The platform exposes a three-layer interface - Python library, REST API, and Model Context Protocol server - so that any building energy tool (EnergyPlus, Home Assistant) can integrate behavioral intelligence without bespoke coupling code. A plugin registry lets the community add new occupant strata, custom schedulers, and alternative memory backends as separate installable packages. Two validation tiers show that ATUS-grounded sampling reproduces empirically calibrated activity distributions and that demographic priors propagate into persona-consistent agent reasoning across timesteps, establishing internal consistency across strata. BuildOcc provides the building energy community with a reusable, openly available implementation of the occupant behavioral layer. BuildOcc is openly released at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21192895 under the Apache License 2.0 and installable via pip install buildocc.

title: AVENUE: Audio-Video EditiNg Understanding and Evaluation
summary: Audio-video (AV) editing aims to modify audio and video content according to a target prompt. Unlike single-modality editing, AV editing requires models to infer a modality-selective edit scope from the prompt alone: determining not only what should change, but also which modality should be preserved. Faithfully evaluating such models therefore requires both (i) benchmarks that span diverse edit types and modality categories, and (ii) evaluation that is itself modality-aware and sample-specific. However, existing AV editing benchmarks provide limited coverage of edit types and modality combinations, while current evaluation systems are often modality-blind and sample-agnostic, making it difficult to assess whether models faithfully preserve the unintended modality. To address these gaps, we introduce AVENUE, Audio-Video EditiNg Understanding and Evaluation, comprising two contributions: (1) a benchmark of 1,291 source clips and 7,957 editing instructions across audio-targeted, video-targeted, and AV-coupled edit types, curated and human-verified from VGGSound; and (2) a sample-specific, modality-aware evaluation framework that specifies, for each sample, both the intended change and the content that must remain intact. We evaluate representative AV editing models spanning three editing paradigms : joint, sequential, and separate, providing the first systematic analysis of modality-selectivity across paradigms. Our findings reveal a fundamental open challenge: when editing one modality, existing models frequently induce unintended changes in the other, regardless of paradigm. AVENUE provides a benchmark and modality-aware evaluation framework to drive progress toward more controllable AV editing models. Our dataset is publicly available on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/datasets/AVENUE-dataset/AVENUE.

title: iBrain: A Unified Foundation Model Reading the Brain from Surface to Spikes
summary: Invasive neural recordings provide high-fidelity measurements of brain activity, with signals such as intracranial EEG (iEEG) and intracortical spiking activity capturing neural dynamics at different spatial and temporal scales. Yet existing neural foundation models have largely been developed independently for different invasive recording paradigms, leaving joint pretraining across heterogeneous invasive signals underexplored. In this work, we introduce iBrain, a unified foundation model that jointly learns from iEEG and spiking activity. iBrain employs signal-specific encoders to accommodate their distinct signal characteristics and a shared spatiotemporal Transformer backbone to model dependencies across recording channels and time. We pretrain iBrain on over 7,000 hours of heterogeneous neural recordings using masked signal reconstruction and channel-view alignment, promoting contextual modeling of neural dynamics and robustness across different channels. iBrain consistently outperforms single-signal pretraining baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks. Further experiments demonstrate that iBrain exhibits transferability and data efficiency across diverse recording settings. These results highlight the potential of joint pretraining on heterogeneous invasive neural recordings to support scalable neural modeling and transferable representations across recording settings and downstream tasks.

title: A Note on Binary Quadratic Systems and their relation to complexity theory
summary:
Deciding whether a system of multivariate quadratic equations over $\mathbb F_2$ has a solution is a classical NP-complete problem, and remains so for square systems, with as many equations as variables. The hardness of this problem is one of the cornerstones of nowadays post-quantum cryptography. Let $\mathrm{MQ}_0(n)$ and $\mathrm{MQ}_1(n)$ denote the sets of square quadratic systems in $n$ variables having respectively no solutions and exactly one solution. $\cup_{n\geq 2} \mathrm{MQ}_0(n)$ is a coNP-complete language, while $\cup_{n\geq 2} \mathrm{MQ}_1(n)$ lies in DP. It is known that $\lim_{n\to \infty} |\mathrm{MQ}_1(n)|/|\mathrm{MQ}_0(n)|=1$. Here we prove the explicit finite-$n$ bounds \[ |\mathrm{MQ}_0(n)|<|\mathrm{MQ}_1(n)| \le \left(1+\frac{1}{2^n-1}\right)|\mathrm{MQ}_0(n)|, \]
  More generally, let $Q_d$ be the space of polynomial functions $(\mathbb{F}_2)^n\to\mathbb F_2$ of degree at most $d$, and let $α_k$ count square systems in $(Q_d)^n$ having exactly $k$ solutions. Then \[ α_0<α_1 \le \left(1+\frac{1}{2^n-1}\right)α_0\,, \qquad 2\le d\le n \,. \] The proof combines matroid and coding-theoretic methods. We interpret $(\mathbb{F}_2)^n$ as the ground set of the evaluation matroid of $Q_d$, express $α_0$ and $α_1$ through characteristic polynomials, and use a Whitney-type sign-reversing involution to show that the only terms that can push $α_1-α_0$ below $α_1/2^n$ come from the elements of a matroid port. These are identified with minimal-support words of the Reed--Muller code $\mathrm{RM}(n-d-1,n)=\mathrm{RM}(d,n)^\perp$; the required estimate then follows from the MacWilliams identity, the minimum-distance bound $2^{d+1}$, and the even-weight structure of the code.

title: On the Parameterized Complexity of Coloring Discovery
comments: 22 pages, 4 figures. Appears in the Proceedings of the 52nd International Conference on Current Trends in Theory and Practice of Computer Science (Sofsem 2027)
summary: Coloring Discovery asks whether a possibly improper initial coloring can be made proper within a prescribed number of allowed changes. We study the parameterized complexity of three modification step models that were studied previously in the literature: recoloring one vertex (color flipping), swapping the colors of arbitrary vertices (color swapping), and swapping colors only across an edge (color sliding). For color flipping, we give exact fixed-parameter algorithms for the parameters vertex cover and distance to complete. For color swapping, we obtain fixed-parameter tractability for the parameter vertex cover plus the number of colors. Our lower bounds show W[1]-hardness for treedepth plus feedback vertex set in the color flipping model and for the number of colors plus bandwidth or distance to disjoint paths in the swapping and sliding models. All three variants remain NP-complete with four colors on graphs of diameter two.
comment: 22 pages, 4 figures. Appears in the Proceedings of the 52nd International Conference on Current Trends in Theory and Practice of Computer Science (Sofsem 2027)

title: Reification as a Transferable Vocabulary: Zero-Shot Link Prediction with Vanilla GNNs
comments: v2 corrects the test graphs of eight benchmarks (see the correction note in Appendix B.9). An extended analysis of what carries the transfer is in preparation. 33 pages, 3 figures. Code and evaluation pipeline: https://github.com/getorbital/REIFM ; checkpoints: https://huggingface.co/itmatr/REIFM
summary: Knowledge graph foundation models such as ULTRA achieve zero-shot link prediction on unseen graphs through dedicated architectures that hard-code a transfer mechanism. In this work we move that mechanism out of the architecture and into the representation, by \emph{reifying} the input graph: every fact becomes a node, connected to its subject, object, and relation type through a fixed vocabulary of six meta-relations, with relation types as anonymous shared nodes rather than model parameters. On this representation, five textbook GNNs (GAT, GINE with sum and with mean+max aggregation, GraphSAGE, R-GCN), each trained on a single knowledge graph of 4,245 triples for 30 minutes on one NVIDIA A100, transfer zero-shot to 40 inductive link-prediction benchmarks. The best of them, an off-the-shelf GAT, matches ULTRA, a dedicated foundation model pretrained on three graphs, across ULTRA's own evaluation suite. The same fixed vocabulary extends to relational databases, a row becoming an entity and a foreign-key column a relation type; a preliminary probe on two unseen databases, with no cell values, schema text or in-context labels, shows a model of this family pretrained on three knowledge graphs ranking foreign-key targets far above random-initialization and degree controls. We release the code, the checkpoints, and the evaluation pipeline for all 40 benchmarks.

title: First Attack, Final Offensive: The Dark Forest on an Open Roster
comments: Add delay by distance and unobserved agents that may help, and drop the assumption of v2 that an unobserved agent who sees a strike can only be provoked by it. 23 pages, 2 figures, 1 table, including appendices
summary: The Dark Forest argument holds that a civilization that detects another should strike it at once. The choice it addresses is general: an agent that has located another nearby must decide whether to strike it, collaborate with it, or do neither, without knowing who else is there. Of sixteen treatments of this decision that we examined, ten assume a known set of players; the other six add unobserved agents only in games in which strikes and replies arrive instantly, in simulations, or in informal arguments. We show that when the roster is open, so that no agent knows even its list of nearby agents to be complete, the course that maximizes an agent's expected survival time if no unobserved agent acts still maximizes it, whatever else the agent believes, if and only if the agent gives at most a threshold probability to an unobserved agent acting, by attacking or helping the agent or by striking the located agent. Without further assumptions the threshold is below one half whatever the course, because an unobserved agent may reply to one course with help and to another with an attack, as soon as an agent as near as the located one could reply. If the agent knows the located agent completely and assumes that it would receive no help from unobserved agents, the threshold for collaboration can approach one. Even below the threshold the agent cannot know that the course it favors is in fact better: however much it knows of the one it has located, some world consistent with all it has observed makes another course better. These results do not apply to an agent that knows all but one of its courses would destroy it. For every other agent, no case for striking first, or for any other course, that assumes nothing about the unobserved agents withstands an even chance that one of them acts: some belief that gives that chance favors another course.

title: Unified CT and MRI Pancreas Segmentation for Label-Efficient Cross-Modality Subregion Transfer
summary: Robust medical image segmentation across imaging modalities is challenging because of large differences in appearance and intensity distributions. Models trained on a single modality often show substantial performance drops when applied to unseen domains. In this work, we develop a unified 3D pancreas segmentation framework that applies domain-adversarial learning to 4,604 heterogeneous CT and MRI scans to learn anatomical representations. A shared nnU-Net encoder-decoder is trained for whole-pancreas segmentation, with a latent domain discriminator encouraging CT-MRI feature alignment. The learned encoder is subsequently transferred to pancreatic head-body-tail segmentation using limited MRI-only subregion annotations. An average Dice score of 87.31% on the in-distribution test set and Dice scores ranging from 84.20% to 88.09% across external OOD datasets were achieved in whole pancreas segmentation. Dice scores of 80.53% on MRI and 83.05% on CT were achieved for downstream subregion segmentation, without using CT subregion annotations. These results demonstrate that a unified anatomical representation can support both cross-modality pancreas segmentation and label-efficient downstream transfer.

title: TryOnReward: Learning Foveated Consistency for Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of Virtual Try-On
summary: Virtual Try-On (VTON) aims to dress a person with the reference garment, producing visually reasonable results aligned with human preferences. Turning this preference-oriented goal into an actionable objective relies on a scoring function aligned with human taste. However, classic fidelity metrics exhibit weak correlation with human judgments, and generic VLMs fail to provide the discriminative granularity demanded by try-on quality evaluation, which hinges on faithfully preserving garment and person details. This shortcoming is further exacerbated in the reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) optimization and leads to severe reward hacking. To this end, we present TryOnReward, a fine-grained reward model tailored for VTON. Built on a vision-language backbone, it adopts a foveation calibration objective that grounds each quality dimension in the relevant region to avoid global shortcut learning. Meanwhile, TryOnReward jointly optimizes pairwise preferences and per-dimension quality scores via margin-aware supervision, leveraging both relative and absolute quality signals. For model training and evaluation, we build TryOnRank-100K, a human-annotated per-dimension rating dataset, alongside TryOn-Bench and TryOnRewardBench, two benchmarks covering diverse real scenarios. Extensive experiments confirm that our proposed TryOnReward significantly outperforms generic judges in human preference alignment, and when serving as the RFT reward function, it consistently yields human-preferred try-on results across multiple baselines.

title: Tabby: An Open Pretraining Recipe for Time Series Foundation Models
summary: In this report, we release Tabby, a long context probabilistic time series foundation model, together with a complete and open recipe of how it was built. Tabby adopts an encoder-only patch Transformer architecture and concentrates the contributions on the data and the training procedure. The pretraining corpus combines an extended real-world collection, GIFT-Eval-Pretrain+ and BLAST, with synthetic data from KernelSynth and CauKerV2, an online generator that composes temporal dynamics through randomly sampled structural causal models. Training couples a progressive convergence schedule, which yields reusable intermediate checkpoints, with a deep quantile supervision objective for intermediate layers. The resulting 145M parameter backbone supports contexts of up to 8,192 observations and serves forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection, while a prompt-tuning module further improves in-distribution forecasting performance with the pretrained weights frozen. Tabby achieves competitive zero-shot forecasting performance on GIFT-Eval and the out-of-distribution TIME benchmark, while the same pretrained backbone also supports classification on the UCR Archive and zero-shot anomaly detection on TSB-AD-U. We release training pipeline and model as open source at huawei-noah/trustworthyAI.

title: Parallel Policy-Gradient Methods for Parameter Optimization of Nonlinear Feedback Controllers
summary: Structured feedback controllers provide stability guarantees, but their performance depends on manually tuned parameters. Policy-gradient methods offer a systematic way to tune these parameters, but evaluating the gradient is computationally expensive because it requires a sequential forward rollout of the state dynamics followed by a backward rollout of the costate dynamics. This letter develops a time-parallel policy-gradient framework for discrete-time nonlinear control-affine systems. We evaluate the policy gradient by formulating the forward state and backward costate rollouts as residual-minimization problems and solving them with Gauss-Newton (GN) iterations that use parallel associative scans. We show that global asymptotic stability and local exponential stability of the closed loop guarantee convergence of the parallel state solver without requiring bounds on Jacobian products throughout the state space. Near the exact trajectory, GN iterations converge quadratically in a neighborhood whose size is independent of the horizon T. When initialized at the equilibrium trajectory, a clipped variant converges at a linear rate that is also independent of T. We also quantify how horizon truncation and solver tolerance affect the accuracy of the policy gradient. Experiments on an LQR problem and a lossless Lorenz-96 system with saturated passivity-based control demonstrate improved closed-loop performance and computational benefits.

title: From Per-Frame Search to Practical Attacks: Investigating Adversarial Robustness of Multi-Agent Heterogeneous Cooperative Perception
summary: Heterogeneous cooperative perception (CP) lets connected agents with different sensors and encoders share bird's-eye-view (BEV) features and align them through learned translation modules before fusion and detection. A malicious collaborator can perturb its broadcast to erase real objects from a neighbor's view, yet prior CP attacks assume homogeneous agents and rely on per-frame gradient descent that needs test-time labels, online detector queries, and slow backward passes. Porting these homogeneous attacks to heterogeneous CP exposes two further architectural barriers. Translation modules often block direct gradients, and heterogeneous fusion stacks use per-location fusion and detection heads that leave the standard removal-loss gradient zero on over $99\%$ of the attacker's message, so per-frame updates reach only the sparse anchor footprint while neighboring cells still detect the object. We present HetPoison, a practical feature attack that trains a convolutional generator once, offline, on a frozen surrogate stack to map channel-observable features to a bounded perturbation in one forward pass, requiring no labels, detector queries, or gradients online. Because the generator parameterizes perturbations across the spatial neighborhood rather than per coordinate, HetPoison overcomes sparse anchor gradients while amortizing search across frames into a $\sim$2 ms forward pass. On OPV2V-H, HetPoison lowers STAMP detection average precision from $0.899$ to $0.063$, outperforms 500-step Adam-PGD on HEAL, STAMP, and CodeFilling at up to $14{,}000\times$ lower online cost, and remains effective on real-world V2X-Real fleets and under cross-family transfer, communication delay, quantization, and unseen collaborator encoders.

title: Large trees of the Sierra Nevada, California: individual delineation and health status over the period 2020--2025 from remotely sensed data
summary: Large trees store a disproportionate share of forest biomass and take centuries to replace, yet their distribution and health status remain unknown at regional scale. Here, we mapped the large trees (crown area $\geq$ 100 m$^2$) of the Sierra Nevada and characterized their health status from 2020 to 2025. Crowns were delineated in a canopy height model derived from 2020 USDA-NAIP aerial images, using a deep learning model trained on 3.3 million synthetic trees. The delineation, validated with 20,273 giant sequoia crowns and hand-drawn crowns without species identification, reached a median IoU of 0.60 after centroid alignment. In total, 6,515,705 large trees were mapped, and their distribution was mainly associated with temperature and precipitation. Colour changes in the visible and near infrared were detected in the Sentinel-2 time series of each crown and used to determine its health status, validated against field observations of 1,015 giant sequoias. Inside the 2020--2024 wildfire perimeters, 61.4\% of the large trees (946,786) were disturbed or dead, against 2.2\% outside. We estimate that $\sim$650,000 large trees, one in ten in the Sierra Nevada, very likely died within these perimeters, mostly in 2020 and 2021. Individual trees can now be monitored over entire regions.

title: LSTM-UT and Bounded Gated Memory for Looped Transformers
summary: Can the loop of a looped Transformer serve as a rollout, with one application of the shared block per step of a dynamical system? We started with two existing designs, one that carries only its residual stream and one, CoTFormer, that also caches every earlier state. On Rule 30, a chaotic cellular automaton, both lose the computation shortly after their trained depth. LSTM-UT, which adds an LSTM-style gated cell, does not, and it recalls earlier states better. Taking it apart shows that each ability has a simpler source. For rollouts it is decay: a fixed decay on the plain model's stream is sufficient. For recall it is an input-dependent gate: at the longest horizon a gated stream with no cell recalls as well as LSTM-UT, and no fixed decay helps. The two do not simply add, since a gated stream with a fixed decay does neither reliably. Storing every earlier state hurts extrapolation, where CoTFormer fits and rolls out further with its cache cut to the most recent repeat; in recall, the stored copy is looked up at the shortest horizon and not at the next. LSTM-UT, whose forget gate makes the decay itself input-dependent, is the only model in the leading group on both. The forget gate was added to the LSTM so that a state carried at weight one could be reset instead of accumulating; we find the same need over depth. In language modelling LSTM-UT is competitive with CoTFormer at lower training cost. Code is available at https://github.com/arskvnc22/lstm-ut

title: Attention Routing Stabilizes Early: Working-Set Inference for Recurrent Language Models
summary: Recurrent-depth language models, such as looped Transformers, repeatedly apply shared network blocks to refine latent representations, enabling additional test-time computation without generating explicit intermediate reasoning tokens. However, recurrent inference repeatedly accesses long contexts: full attention incurs quadratic computation during prefill, while autoregressive decoding repeatedly reads large key-value (KV) caches, introducing substantial memory traffic and capacity pressure. We study how attention routing evolves across recurrent depth and uncover a consistent separation in convergence timescales: routing-related quantities, including the attention support and the attention distribution, stabilize substantially earlier than representation-related quantities such as hidden states and attention outputs. This suggests a two-stage structure in which the model discovers a sparse working set and then refines representations over largely the same routing support. Motivated by this structure, we introduce WISE (Working-set Inference with Support Exploitation), a training-free method that uses unrestricted global attention during early recurrent steps to discover a block-structured working set, and then reuses it as the routing support in later steps while keeping recurrent refinement and within-support attention computation dynamic. By combining sparse recurrent attention with compact KV-cache management, WISE reduces both redundant attention computation and memory movement during inference. Across reasoning and long-context benchmarks, WISE closely approaches full-attention accuracy on key evaluated workloads while outperforming early-static support baselines. At 64K context, our implementation achieves up to a 6.46x decode throughput improvement under GPU memory pressure. Our code is available at https://github.com/tbn5pj/WISE_code.

title: Parameterized Enumeration of Minimal Defensive Alliances
comments: Appears in the Proceedings of the 52nd International Conference on Current Trends in Theory and Practice of Computer Science (Sofsem 2027)
summary: In this paper, we consider the complexity of enumerating inclusion minimal defensive alliances. We present a polynomial-delay algorithm on graphs with maximum degree 5. We complement this result by proving that there is no output-polynomial algorithm on bipartite graphs with maximum degree 6 and degeneracy 2, unless P = NP. Furthermore, there is an \FPT-delay algorithm when parameterized by neighborhood diversity. This result is the first exploit of a recently published enumeration algorithm for ILPs. By way in contrast, we prove that, for the parameter pathwidth, there is no FPT-delay algorithm for enumerating all inclusion minimal defensive alliances (unless FPT = W[1]). This is the first non-enumerability result using parameterized complexity for variations of Another/Next-problems.
comment: Appears in the Proceedings of the 52nd International Conference on Current Trends in Theory and Practice of Computer Science (Sofsem 2027)

title: Relative Discharge Stage Classification from Battery Sensor Measurements in Laboratory Discharge Tests
summary: Relative discharge stage (RDS) is an ordinal target obtained by dividing the realized remaining discharge time by the total duration of the same discharge episode and assigning the ratio to a bin. We investigate whether these bins can be predicted from measurements available up to the present sample. The framework combines an electrothermal equivalent-circuit model and adaptive extended Kalman filter to estimate state of charge (SOC), then classifies discharge stage using the estimated SOC, current, terminal voltage, and surface temperature. With the evaluated two-layer convolutional network, the final-time prediction directly uses the three most recent observations. Earlier measurements can influence the output through the recursive SOC estimate. On complete discharge tests, the five-stage classifier achieved accuracies of 95.38% and 81.23% for FTP-75 and PDMHC and 76.41% and 73.87% for LCO_5 and LCO_6, respectively. These results characterize classification within the laboratory protocols. Incremental value over SOC alone, reference-based SOC accuracy, and utility in vehicle operation remain to be established.

title: Even Sharper Bounds for Transductive Learning and Its Applications
summary: We introduce Sharper Transductive Local Complexity (STLC) as a new tool for improving current transductive bounds. Although Local Rademacher Complexity (LRC) has been used to obtain sharp inductive generalization bounds and local-complexity-based transductive bounds, it has remained open whether a localized Rademacher-complexity framework can achieve the same fixed-point and confidence structure as its inductive counterpart. STLC provides an affirmative answer to this question. STLC is constructed by first deriving a new Bernstein-type concentration inequality for the test-train process, under uniform sampling without replacement. The proof uses a new two-parameter entropy argument based on the modified log-Sobolev inequality for the swap walk. A subsequent peeling strategy with a surrogate localization functional yields transductive excess-risk bounds that match the fixed-point and confidence structure of the classical LRC-based inductive bounds without the additional logarithmic confidence gap in existing works. We further advance transductive learning through two applications. First, for realizable transductive learning over a binary-valued class of VC dimension $2\le d <\infty$ with $u\ge m\ge d$, where $u$ and $m$ are the test and training sizes, STLC gives the upper bound $O(d\log(me/d)/m}$. This rate matches the classical LRC-based, standard ERM-style inductive upper bound. It remains a logarithmic factor $\log(me/d)$ above both the optimal realizable inductive PAC rate and the transductive minimax lower bound, which are of order $d/m$. Our prior work achieves the excess risk of $O(d/m)$ in a transductive setup by randomized learning. Second, STLC gives a sharper, spectrum-adaptive excess-risk bound for transductive kernel learning than the prior local-complexity-based result.

title: Reducing Fixed-Batch Client Idleness in Many-Client Edge Split Learning
comments: 12 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Extended version of v1 under a new title, with two additional authors. Corrects the accuracy values and target rounds of the schedule-accounted CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 studies: v1 reported a batch-averaged macro accuracy. The real-execution measurements are unchanged
summary: Parallel Split Learning with Global Sampling (GPSL) trains a split model on a fixed-size batch drawn from the data of all clients. When the client population is much larger than the batch, most clients contribute no data in a round, and additional server capacity does not change this. We propose Global Clustered Parallel Split Learning (GCPSL), which assigns clients to stable clusters, runs one GPSL workload per cluster concurrently, and periodically fuses the split-model replicas. We derive the expected direct data participation under the batch sampler, which separates repeated sampling of the same clients from idling at the fusion barrier. With 256 clients, more clusters raise participation but reduce the client diversity seen by each workload. In three paired runs on four H100 GPUs, GCPSL raises direct data participation from 22% to 57-60%. With random or size-balanced clusters, it reaches 85% CIFAR-10 validation accuracy in 5.7 minutes, 1.6 times faster than GPSL with its batch sharded across the same GPUs. It matches per-step synchronized data-parallel GPSL at 85% and reaches 88% in about 10 instead of 19.5 minutes, without per-step global gradient or BatchNorm synchronization. Concurrent execution is 3.11 times faster than sequential execution of the same workloads.
